amendments.rule: The BSB comparison and Strong's numbers are secondary evidence, and neither an ASV italic nor a reference alignment overrides direct analysis of the Hebrew. **An ASV marginal note is read on exactly those terms.** The packet prints the edition's own notes beneath each verse — an alternative rendering (*Or, Send forth*, *Or, in*, *Or, spirit*, *Or, For*) and a literal gloss of the Hebrew (*Hebrew upon the face of the waters*) — and what is aligned is the text as printed, never the margin. A word the margin would have written is not a target token and licenses nothing; a construction the margin prefers does not move a unit, an edge or a head; and a preposition the margin renders one way keeps the word the printed text renders it by, so `בַּדָּרוֹם` → *toward the south* aligns *toward* to the `בְּ` whatever the margin offers. Such a note may corroborate an analysis the Hebrew already carries, exactly as an ASV italic may under rule 7: a literal gloss showing that a preposition and its construct noun were rendered by a single English word supports the fusion rule 30 finds there, and the absence of a note is not evidence against anything. But it decides nothing, and where the note and the printed text point different ways the printed text governs. Where a reader might otherwise wonder, say in the unit's note that the margin was read and set aside.
amendments.why: Rule 38 is the contract's statement of what is not evidence, and it names the BSB, Strong's, italics and reference alignments but says nothing about the ASV's own margins — which the packet prints beneath the verse, so every verse pass sees them and has no ruling to apply. Six of this chapter's ten verses carry one, and two of them would change an alignment if followed: 11.3's *Or, in* against the printed *toward* on the `בְּ`, and 11.8's *Or, and remember* against the printed *but* on the waw. The chapter set them all aside and used only the 11.1 literal gloss, as corroboration of a fusion rule 30 already rules. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule because the ruling belongs beside the italic and the BSB in rule 38; a separate rule would leave rule 38 reading as a closed list to whoever reaches it first. Nothing in the corpus bears against it, and the addition changes no existing sentence of the rule.

conventions: Disjunctive protasis `אִם … וְאִם` where the ASV writes one connective for the waw and the repeated particle together (11.3: `וְאִם בַּצָּפוֹן` → *or toward the north*): the waw takes the written *or* and the repeated `אִם` is its own `unrepresented` unit, on rule 26's reasoning for `בֵּין X וּבֵין Y` — the connective is not transferred to the repeated element — with rule 22 for the repetition. The competing reading gives the *or* to `אִם` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and BSB aligns it that way; the corpus supports both (waw → *or* in 240 units, `אִם` → *or* in 33), so this is a chapter reading rather than a settled one. Where the ASV writes a word for each morpheme instead, as at 11.6 (*or whether*), each takes its own and nothing is repeated.

Six of the ten verses carry ASV marginal notes — alternative renderings at 11.1 (*Send forth*), 11.2 (*Divide … into seven*), 11.3 (*in*, twice), 11.5 (*spirit*), 11.8 (*For*, *and remember*) and 11.10 (*vexation*), and a literal gloss at 11.1 (*Hebrew upon the face of the waters*). Every unit aligns the text as printed. The 11.1 gloss was used only as corroboration that `עַל־פְּנֵי` was rendered by one English word, which rule 30 already rules a fusion; no margin moved an edge or a head, and 11.3 keeps the printed *toward* on its `בְּ` rather than the marginal *in*.

report: Checked all 28 candidate lemma groups; none is a split. The article group (24 occurrences) is aligned wherever the ASV writes a *the* and unrepresented wherever it writes none — 11.1 s011 (*after many days*), 11.5 s026 (bare *all*), 11.8 s006 (*a man*), 11.9 s034 (bare *God*), 11.9 s037 (*into judgment*), 11.10 s014 (bare *youth*). The chapter counts its construct chains consistently: `דֶּרֶךְ הָרוּחַ` (11.5) writes a *the* before each word, so each morpheme takes the one standing before its own, while `מַעֲשֵׂה הָאֱלֹהִים` (11.5) and `יְמֵי הַחֹשֶׁךְ` (11.8) render the rectum anarthrously and front the single *the* onto the article. That is rule 29 dividing two shapes, not two analyses of one.

The waw group (*and*, *or*, *but*, *yea*, *Truly*, *Therefore*) is rule 14's open list read off the ASV, and every one of those words stands written in its verse. `בְּ` takes *in*, *toward*, *into*, *after*, *upon* where a word is written and is unrepresented once, at 11.4 s007, where the ASV promotes its object to the direct object of *regardeth* — rule 40's condition, not a second treatment. `לְ` → *to* (11.2 s003) beside *unto* (11.2 s007) is two words the ASV wrote for two morphemes inside one verse.

The one construction written in two shapes is the disjunctive protasis `אִם … וְאִם`. At 11.3 the ASV writes a single connective for the pair (*or toward the north*): the chapter gives it to the waw and marks the repeated `אִם` (s018) unrepresented. At 11.6 it writes two (*or whether*), and each morpheme takes its own. The 11.3 division follows rule 26's ruling on `בֵּין X וּבֵין Y` — do not transfer the connective to the repeated element, the waw is what licenses it — together with rule 22 for the repetition. The corpus lets either morpheme carry an *or* (waw → *or* in 240 units, `אִם` → *or* in 33), so this is a reading to record, not a rule to promote; it is logged as a convention with the competing reading named.

The candidate table is blind to `added` units, so I read the dump for them directly. There are three, all in 11.5 and 11.7, and each stands where no morpheme licenses the English: the italic *nor* of 11.5 opens a phrase with no conjunction morpheme in it (rule 14's closing sentence), the italic *do grow* is a wholly supplied lexical predicate (rule 20), and the *it* of *a pleasant thing it is … to behold* is rule 20's cleft dummy, named there by example. Nothing comparable is folded into a neighbouring word elsewhere in the chapter: 11.5 keeps the non-italic *how* on the comparative `כְּ`, the only morpheme standing for it, and 11.7 keeps the copula *is* on the predicate `טוֹב` beside the added *it*.

Two head choices carrying a named competing reading were re-checked and stand: 11.9 s002 `בָּחוּר` → *O young man* headed on *man* under rule 31's tie sentence, and 11.3 s009 `יָרִיקוּ` → *they empty themselves*, where *themselves* renders the Hiphil's own sense rather than supplying an object, as rule 44 keeps *yourselves* with `הִגְדִּיל`. Both are judgment calls the verse notes already record.

BSB: none of the three disagreement families is an error. The five Td disagreements are all articles for which the ASV writes no *the*, which BSB attaches to the host word by its documented convention. The 11.4 `בֶ` is rule 40's silenced preposition, which BSB attaches to its phrase. The 11.3 `אִם` is the disjunctive above, where BSB gives the *or* to the particle and this chapter gives it to the waw — a convention difference the corpus does not settle, not a correction. No accepted edge was moved to improve the rate.
